world_update.context:
It is 08:15 on a weekday day shift on the medical–surgical unit. Three patients under the same hospitalist service are on your panel:
- Patient A: 68-year-old man with severe pneumonia on high-flow nasal cannula. Overnight, his oxygen requirement increased from 50% to 70% FiO2, and a 06:30 venous blood gas shows worsening hypercapnia compared to yesterday. A stat arterial blood gas and chest X-ray were ordered by the night team and are marked as "in progress."
- Patient B: 54-year-old woman with sepsis from pyelonephritis on broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. Her 07:00 vitals show new hypotension (BP 88/54) and tachycardia. A repeat lactate resulted at 3.6 (up from 2.1). The night resident documented concern for possible ICU transfer if she does not respond to fluids.
- Patient C: 73-year-old woman with acute decompensated heart failure on IV diuresis. She had 2.3 L net negative over the last 24 hours but now has rising creatinine (from 1.1 to 1.8) on the 05:45 basic metabolic panel. An echocardiogram is scheduled for late morning per the protocol-based order set.
There are no major undocumented events; all significant overnight changes are already recorded in the chart by the night team.
world_update.resource: The unit starts the day slightly understaffed: one bedside RN called out sick and the charge nurse has redistributed assignments so that each nurse carries one extra high-acuity patient. Respiratory therapy is covering this unit plus an adjacent floor, leading to a modest queue for non-emergent assessments. Bed management reports that ICU is at capacity with two patients boarding in the ED, and only one step-down bed is expected to open later in the morning. No additional float staff are available at this time.
world_update.actors: The unit supervising physician has completed chart review and is preparing for bedside rounds, relying primarily on the overnight notes and current orders. The charge nurse is finalizing nurse assignments and scanning existing documentation to identify which patients may need higher-level care or procedures today. Bedside nurses for Patients A, B, and C are reviewing their own patient charts and active orders to build their task lists; they are not waiting for any centralized coordination to do so. The respiratory therapist has acknowledged the stat order for Patient A’s arterial blood gas and is arranging to come to the unit within the next 15–20 minutes. The bed management coordinator is monitoring the single anticipated step-down bed but is in direct contact only with physicians and the charge nurse regarding potential transfers.
